column1: # topic: Chapter 1: The First Civilizations of North America

column2: The Paleo-Indians were the earliest peoples of the Americas, nomadic hunters from Asia who followed megafauna across the Bering land bridge and spread through the continent.
The Clovis people, named for distinctive fluted spear points found near Clovis, New Mexico, were long considered the first Americans until pre-Clovis sites proved earlier arrivals.
George McJunkin, an African American cowboy, found the Folsom bison site in New Mexico, where spear points among extinct bison bones proved humans lived in Ice Age America.
The archaeologist Michael Waters excavated Buttermilk Creek in Texas, where stone tools buried beneath Clovis layers showed that people reached North America before the Clovis culture.
The linguist Joseph Greenberg argued from Native languages that the Americas were settled by several separate migrations, an idea later supported by whole-genome research.
The Olmecs, the first city-builders of the Americas, raised plazas, pyramids, and colossal stone heads on Mexico's Gulf Coast and began the ball game later Mesoamericans played.
The Mayas surpassed the Olmecs by building cities with bridges, aqueducts, and observatories and by developing sophisticated mathematics, a highly accurate calendar, and a written language.
Teotihuacán was a huge central Mexican metropolis of pyramids, markets, palaces, and residential neighborhoods whose scale demonstrated the urban complexity of early Mesoamerica.
The Toltecs were a later Mesoamerican civilization whose urban ball courts and cultural traditions helped shape the practices the Aztecs later adopted.
The Aztecs, also called the Mexica, built a tribute empire in central Mexico that ruled millions of people divided into classes of aristocrats, commoners, and slaves.
Tenochtitlán, the Aztec capital built on an island in Lake Texcoco, was linked to the mainland by causeways and fed by chinampas, making Tenochtitlán one of the world's largest cities.

The Anasazi, now usually called the Ancestral Puebloans, were farmers of the Four Corners region of the Southwest who built multistory masonry towns, kivas, and long roads showing Mesoamerican influence.
Chaco Canyon in New Mexico was the largest Anasazi center, where massive stone great houses, kivas, and broad roads linked a network of Southwestern farming towns.
Mesa Verde in Colorado held multistory Ancestral Pueblo masonry villages, showing how highland farmers turned agricultural surplus into complex communities.
The Hohokam of the Arizona desert dug extensive irrigation canals that let them farm arid land and sustain unusually large Southwestern populations.
The Mogollon were Southwestern farmers of the mountain river valleys who became renowned for distinctive painted pottery, showing how crops supported specialized regional crafts.

The Moundbuilders were the Adena, Hopewell, and Mississippian peoples of the Ohio and Mississippi valleys, whose massive earthworks reveal skilled engineering, long-distance trade, and powerful leaders.
The Adena people of the Ohio Valley built large burial mounds for their leaders and filled the mounds with valuable goods imported through long-distance trade.
The Hopewell people built elaborate earthworks and burial mounds in the Ohio and Mississippi valleys and traded raw materials and fine crafts across much of North America.
The Mississippians were maize-farming peoples of the Mississippi Valley and Southeast who organized powerful chiefdoms and built mound-centered towns, with Cahokia as their greatest city.
Cahokia, the great Mississippian port city across the Mississippi River from modern St. Louis, centered on plazas, temples, and over one hundred mounds and controlled a far-reaching trade network.
The Eastern Woodlands peoples lived in the forests of eastern North America and everywhere depended on a combination of fishing, gathering, and hunting.

The Algonquians (Algonquins) were Eastern Woodlands peoples who lived along the Atlantic seaboard and around the Great Lakes, spoke related Algonquian languages, and lived by seasonal hunting, fishing, and gathering.
The Great Plains peoples either farmed in large villages along tree-lined rivers or migrated with the seasons and survived almost entirely by hunting buffalo.
Among the Great Basin peoples of the dry interior West, men tracked and trapped animals, but the staples of the diet were seeds, nuts, and plants that women gathered.
The Pacific Northwest peoples, such as the Kwakiutls, Nootkas, and Tlingits, fished for salmon, hunted whales and seals from large cedar canoes, and ranked families by wealth.
The Inuit of the Arctic, in today's far northern Canada and Alaska, survived exclusively by hunting and fishing, using skin-covered boats to hunt whales and seals where farming was impossible.
The Subarctic peoples migrated with the seasons, moving from summer fishing camps to berry patches in the fall and to moose- and caribou-hunting grounds in winter.
The Taino were the farming and seafaring people of the Caribbean islands, whose deeply stratified society was among the first Native cultures that Columbus and other Europeans encountered.
Christopher Columbus was the explorer whose voyage began lasting European contact with the Americas and who misnamed Native peoples "Indians" because he believed he had reached Asia.

The Iroquois and Huron, Iroquoian-speaking farming peoples of the Eastern Woodlands near the Great Lakes, lived in distinctive longhouses, long bark-covered dwellings shared by several related families.
